"They said news passes through five filters," he told the table. "Five of them. And the first filter is ownership. Who owns the outlet."

Lauren put her spoon down. "Who owns the Ledger?"

He had already looked it up, that afternoon, in the library's business database, and he had the fact ready the way you hold a stone you intend to throw and then discover you might not want to. "The same company that owns the quarry. Not secretly. It's in the filings. Nobody hides it, it's just boring, so nobody says it."

The kitchen went quiet enough that the refrigerator hum became audible, a small persistent noise Lauren realized she had been hearing her whole life without once listening. Her mother said, "I buy that paper every Thursday," in a voice that suggested she was taking inventory of something larger than four dollars a month. Lauren thought of Ms. Sow's immunology unit last spring, the way a body learns a pathogen and keeps the memory; she felt something like that happening to her now, a permanent marking. But being immunized was not the same as being cured, and she understood that even as it happened.

"Okay," she said slowly, working it out between the two of them, her mother's shrug and Adriel's book. "So the Ledger isn't lying. The dust numbers are real, or at least they're printed. It's more like the paper's been cauterized. The wound closed over, and everything looks smooth, and the part that could still bleed just isn't in there." She heard how strange it sounded and kept going anyway. "I don't know if my letter got rejected because of that or because it wasn't good enough. Maybe both. I can't prove which."

"That's the honest version," Adriel said. "I can't prove it either. But the ownership is just a fact. You can print that."

Her mother was already clearing the soup bowls, but she paused. "There's a copier at the clinic. Twenty cents a page."

They stayed at the table past the dishes going cold, Adriel pulling the filings up on his phone, Lauren writing the first line by hand on the back of her rejection letter: Who owns your newspaper? She wrote it, crossed it out, wrote it again.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: The development typically breaks the exposition's themes into short fragments and moves them quickly through several keys, which gives the section its restless sound.
story:
Anais would like it stated, first of all, that she did not need Mr. Clarke's help, and that she only asked for it because her mother kept hovering in the kitchen doorway with her arms crossed like a subpoena had arrived. It had not. What had arrived was her grade report, one D in Music Theory, and her mother's opinion that asking for help was nothing to stigmatize, which was exactly the kind of thing her mother said while making it feel like the opposite.

"It's one assignment," Anais said, spreading the score across the kitchen table. The Mozart was open to the first movement of the K. 332, and her pencil marks on it looked, even to her, like the work of someone guessing. "I'll fix it this weekend."

"Mr. Clarke said you could come by Saturday."

"Mr. Clarke said a lot of things." His comment on her last analysis had been scathing, one line in red at the bottom, and she had read it four times and then folded the page into her back pocket where it still lived, soft at the creases.

Her mother set down a mug of tea and did not leave. So Anais put in one earbud, out of politeness, and pressed play, and let the exposition roll over her. She had learned the labels weeks ago: exposition, where the themes are laid out; development, where things fall apart; recapitulation, where they come home. She had written all three words on her paper. The problem was that she had written them in the wrong places, which was the specific thing Mr. Clarke's red line had pointed out, in his handwriting like a fence.

The music started again from the beginning, and this time she followed with her finger on the staves. The opening tune was polite, almost silly, a little turn and a trill like someone smoothing a skirt. Then came a second theme, singing, in a different key. Then, around measure forty, everything changed. The piano writing turned fast and low, hands chasing, and Anais felt her stomach do the thing it did before a test, the small dropping feeling. She had marked this section as a new theme. She had even named it, in the margin, "third theme, stormy."

Ayden had said something about this section on Thursday, leaning across the aisle with his own score. "It's not new," he had said. "Listen to the first four notes again. Then listen to the middle." She had told him she was fine, thanks, and turned back to her phone, because accepting help from Ayden felt like losing to Ayden, and she was already losing to enough people that week.

But now, alone, with her mother pretending to wash a clean mug at the sink, she dragged the track back. First four notes: turn, rise, little trill. Then she jumped to the stormy middle and listened with her eyes shut, and there it was, buried, broken into pieces, the tune's opening turn tossed between the hands, each fragment landing somewhere new, a different key each time it surfaced, no sooner arrived than flung somewhere else. It was like seeing someone she knew in a crowd, except the person was running and the crowd kept shifting underneath them.

"Oh," she said, out loud, into the kitchen.

Her mother turned off the tap. "Something good?"

"Kind of." Anais pulled out the earbud and held it up like evidence. "The middle section, the part I got wrong. It's not new material. It takes the opening theme and smashes it into these little fragments and moves them through a bunch of keys really fast. That's why it sounds like that. Restless. I called it a third theme and Mr. Clarke called me..." She stopped, then went on, because withholding it was its own kind of lying. "He wrote that I had 'mistaken motion for meaning,' which honestly is the kind of thing that deserves a lawsuit."

Her mother laughed, and Anais did too, surprising herself. Then she took out the folded page from her back pocket, unfolded it on the table next to the score, and read the whole comment for the first time instead of just the last line. The first half said her writing about the second theme showed real sensitivity. The scathing part was only the end, and she had been carrying it around like it was the entire document.

She erased her margin note, "third theme, stormy," and the eraser smeared it gray instead of removing it, so the old guess stayed visible under the new one, which was somehow fitting. She wrote: fragments of the opening theme, moving quickly through several keys. She was not sure yet exactly where the development gave way to the recapitulation, whether it was at the return of the first theme or two bars before it, and she underlined nothing, and left a small question mark, because Mr. Clarke had also written, further up, that a question mark was worth more than a wrong certainty, and she had skipped that sentence the first four times she read the page.

"I'm going to email him," she said. "Not to apologize. Just to say I found it, the theme, in the middle part. And to ask about the one spot."

Her mother dried her hands and finally left the doorway, and Anais put the earbud back in and played the stormy section once more, finger resting on the smeared gray where her old answer used to be, listening for the tune as it surfaced, vanished, and surfaced again somewhere new.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Binary search works only on sorted data: it compares the target with the middle item and throws away the half of the list that cannot contain it.
story:
The computer lab smelled of warm dust and lemon cleaner, and the radiator under the window ticked like something counting down. Nicholas sat two seats from Teo, who was hunched over the attendance program for the robotics club, muttering at his screen. The club had ninety-three members now, and the coach had asked for a quick way to look up any name, so Teo had spent the whole period writing a search that checked the middle of the list first.

"It's elegant," Teo said, spinning his chair around. "You look at the middle name, and if the one you want comes after it, you throw away the whole first half. If it comes before, you throw away the second half. Then you do it again on whatever's left."

Louis-Felix leaned over from the next row, chewing the cap of a pen. "Then why does it keep telling me Priya Rao doesn't exist? She's standing in the hallway. I can see her through the door."

Teo scrolled. He typed Priya's name again. The program printed not found. He typed Mateo Jimenez, who had joined in September, and got not found again, then found for a boy who had left the school in October. Louis-Felix laughed the way people laugh when something is broken and it isn't theirs.

Nicholas pulled his chair over. He had a habit, when something confused him, of holding two ideas side by side until one of them gave way, and now he held Teo's method in one hand and the list in the other. Teo's method assumed something. It assumed that everything before the middle came before it alphabetically, everything after came after. Nicholas scrolled down the member list himself, and near the top, third from the beginning, sat Williamson, Aaron, entered by some volunteer who hadn't cared. Below him, out of order, came a jumble of names typed in whatever sequence people had signed up.

"It only works on sorted data," Nicholas said quietly. "That's the whole thing. It compares the target with the middle item and throws away the half that can't contain it. But if the list isn't sorted, you might throw away the half that does."

Teo stared at the screen. His mouth opened, closed. He scrolled to Williamson, Aaron, third from the top, and put both hands over his face. Louis-Felix said something about an antiquated clipboard being more reliable than ninety-three lines of chaos, and Ms. Silva, who had been watering the fern by the printer, drifted over and asked only whether they wanted the lab open after last bell. She never explained things; she just unlocked doors.

The problem was that sorting cost something. Nicholas knew it the way he knew most things, half by instinct and half by dread: a sort would take time to write, and the list got new names every week, and whoever added them would have to add them in the right place, forever, or the search would start lying again. He felt a small foreboding, the kind he got when a solution opened onto more work than the problem had. It would have been simpler to check every name one by one, top to bottom, slow but honest, impossible to break. But ninety-three names would become two hundred by spring, and the slow honest way would get slower while the fast fragile way stayed fast, as long as someone guarded the fragility.

They stayed until the custodian's cart squeaked past the doorway. Louis-Felix read names aloud from the printed sheet while Teo retyped them in order, and Nicholas wrote the sort, deleting more than he kept, the lab going blue with dusk around them. Once, he thought about how his history teacher liked to historicize everything, to set each problem in its time, and he thought this one had a time too: this particular hour, these three boys, this radiator ticking while a list became orderly. He didn't say it out loud. It would have sounded like something said to be heard.

When they finished, Priya Rao came up on the screen instantly, and Teo made a small sound, half triumph and half embarrassment, and Nicholas understood that the program worked now and would only keep working if someone remembered why. Teo saved the file twice, then a third time to a second drive, and closed the lid gently, the way you close something you no longer entirely trust yourself with.

"Same time Thursday," Teo said. "New members are signing up at lunch."

Nicholas looked at the fern, the dark window, his own reflection ghosted over the code. "I'll come," he said, and zipped his bag.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: The Framingham Heart Study, which began following residents of Framingham, Massachusetts in 1948, gave medicine the term 'risk factor' for habits and conditions that raise later disease risk.
story:
The parking structure was full by ten, so Hudson's grandfather let them out at the curb and circled the block while Hudson queued behind a group of high school juniors wearing matching lanyards. He had one form in his jacket pocket, a program declaration for the university's accelerated health sciences track, and it was due to Ms. Ferreira by five o'clock, since she had agreed to fax it from the school office before the office closed for the weekend. The form had two boxes. Pre-medicine, or undeclared. His mother had already told the relatives he was going to be a doctor.

At the check-in tent he found Alia and Leanne, who had driven up separately and had commandeer a table in the student union for their pamphlets and their coffee. Leanne was there for the creative writing department and had no patience for the health sciences building. "You could just not decide," she said, arranging her brochures by color. "Undeclared is a real thing. People do it." Alia said nothing, which Hudson had learned meant she had an opinion she was saving.

The first session he attended was in a lecture hall with seats that folded down on hinges. A graduate student was presenting a poster about longitudinal cohort studies, and one graph on it showed a curve that climbed and then flattened, approaching some line it never reached, the line labeled with a word Hudson half remembered from pre-calculus: an asymptote. The graduate student kept referring to "the Framingham Heart Study," which began following residents of Framingham, Massachusetts in 1948, and which had given medicine the term "risk factor" for habits and conditions that raise later risk of disease. Hudson copied the phrase into his phone. He did not raise his hand.

He found his grandfather outside the hall, sitting on a bench with the car keys in his fist. His grandfather had driven trucks for thirty-one years and had survived two bypass surgeries, and at the mention of the word Framingham he sat forward. "That's the town," he said. "They tracked a whole town out there. That's why the doctors ask me about my habits now, my smoking years ago, all of it. They call those things risk factors." He said it the way he reported a weather forecast, without editorializing, and then he asked whether Hudson had eaten.

Hudson had not. He bought two hot dogs from the cart, and he and his grandfather ate them on the steps of the statistics building, which was the building Hudson had photographed on the website at two in the morning three weeks ago and told no one about. His grandfather asked which program the second building was, and Hudson said it was the math department, and his grandfather nodded and did not ask the follow-up question. A disaffected student in a department T-shirt sat on the railing nearby, telling anyone who would listen that the rankings were rigged and that it didn't matter where you went. Hudson noticed that Leanne had stopped to argue with him.

Inside the statistics building there was an open lab with screens showing a traffic simulation and a display about disease modeling, and a professor was letting visitors adjust a slider that changed a probability and watching the simulated outbreak shrink or spread. Hudson moved the slider twice. The professor said the model was crude, that real estimates came from decades of records, from people willing to be counted for most of their lives. Hudson thought about a whole town being followed since 1948, before his grandfather had started driving trucks, before his grandfather had started smoking, before anyone knew to ask.

At three o'clock he sat with Alia on the wall by the fountain and laid out what he had. The health sciences track was a straight line, the kind his mother could describe at Thanksgiving. The statistics department was the thing he actually read about at two in the morning, and it was also, he had realized in the lab, not a rejection of the first thing. The study in Framingham was numbers as much as it was medicine. He could learn the one to do the other, or he could find out in two years that he had guessed wrong. "You're allowed to not know," Alia said. "That's what the undeclared box is for." He said the undeclared box was still a decision, which she conceded.

At the fax machine in the school office, Ms. Ferreira read the form before feeding it through. "You're sure?" she said. "I can't unfax it." Hudson looked at the two boxes. He thought of the curve climbing toward its asymptote, close but never touching, and thought that was probably the honest version of being sure. He took out his pen and checked undeclared, and handed the form back, and stood listening to the machine's thin mechanical screech while Ms. Ferreira watched the confirmation page crawl out.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A journal's impact factor, devised by Eugene Garfield, is the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years.
story:
The library closed at nine, and Alex had until nine a.m. tomorrow to submit the review, so he spread his betrayal across half a table: two photocopied articles, the assignment sheet, a notebook with more crossed-out lines than kept ones. Both articles tackled the same question, whether the standard phylogeny of anole lizards held up against newer genetic sampling, and both disagreed, which was the point. He was supposed to compare them, weigh their arguments, and take a position. What he had instead were eleven false starts.

Marwa slid into the chair across from him with two teas from the machine by the entrance and set one at his elbow without comment. She was better at deadlines than he was; she had finished her own review on Tuesday. "Still nothing?" she asked.

"They contradict each other and I can't figure out which one to trust." He turned one photocopy toward her. "This one's from a huge journal, everybody cites it. The other one I've never heard of, but the methods section is twice as long. They sequenced more populations. But the big one's author is famous, like, people lionize him at conferences, apparently."

Merrick arrived ten minutes later, damp from the rain, shaking water off his jacket onto the carpet until Marwa pointed at the umbrella stand. He dropped into the third chair and pulled the famous article toward himself. "Oh, this one. Easy. This is the better paper, obviously."

"How do you know?" Alex asked.

"It's in the journal with the impact factor of like eleven," Merrick said. "The other one's is under two. Higher number, better journal, better article. That's how it works."

Alex looked at the number printed at the bottom of the first page, which he had honestly not even noticed until now. "What does that actually count, though?"

"Citations," Merrick said. "It's how you tell."

"Tell what?"

Merrick waved a hand, the gesture of someone who had never had to say it out loud. "Whether it's good."

Mr. Francis, the reference librarian, was reshelving along the far wall, and Alex caught his eye the way students did when they needed the copier unjammed or the study room unlocked. He came over. Alex explained the assignment, the two articles, Merrick's verdict. He didn't ask a question exactly; he just laid the two first pages side by side and left a silence where the question would go.

Mr. Francis pulled out a chair but didn't sit. "Do you know what an impact factor measures?" he asked Merrick.

"Quality of the journal," Merrick said, with incipient doubt, the kind that shows up a second before you're wrong.

"Garfield devised it," Mr. Francis said. "It's the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years. That's all it is. It's an average over the journal. It doesn't follow an individual article anywhere."

Merrick frowned at the ceiling, doing the arithmetic of his own claim and finding it short. "So a paper in the fancy journal could still be worse than the obscure one."

"That's not for me to say," Mr. Francis said, and went back to his cart, because he was the kind of librarian who believed people should arrive at things themselves.

Alex sat with it. The famous paper was brisk, confident, two pages of interpretation riding on older data. The obscure one was slower, careful, and its lead author was a graduate student. He read both methods sections again, this time with a pen, marking every place the big paper assumed something the small paper had actually tested. The small paper's figures were uglier, hand-labeled, clearly built by someone with no design budget. He started a new draft, and the opening sentence came out whole: the two papers ask the same question but do not stand on the same evidence, and only one of them shows its work.

"You're going with the no-name one," Merrick said, not quite a question.

"I'm going with its evidence," Alex said. "The famous guy might still be right. The new sampling could turn out to be a fluke, or the sample sizes could be too thin for the claims they're making from it. I can't resolve that from here." He wrote that part down too, the uncertainty, because the assignment said a considered position and he was starting to think a considered position included the seams.

Marwa read the draft over his shoulder while he typed, pointing out one paragraph that said the same thing twice and one place where he'd credited an argument to the wrong author. She circled the clock with her finger. Eight-forty. He attached the file, checked the citation format twice, and hit submit with four minutes before the library closed, and Merrick carried his umbrella to the stand on the way out without being told.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
story:
The radiator under the third-floor window of Lab 2B clanked all through November, and Elijah had begun to think of it as a member of the class, a dull-witted tutor who taught only one lesson at unpredictable intervals. On the day of the equilibrium unit, Mr. Crowchild set a beaker of pale blue solution on the warm sill beside it and another on the counter by the door, where the draft pooled, and said only, "Watch them. Write down what you notice, not what you think you should notice." Then he sat at his desk and marked quizzes, apparently content to be useless.

Elijah wanted the scholarship. That was the want underneath everything now, the thing that made him stay after last bell and rewrite labs until his handwriting looked like someone else's, someone surer. The chemistry exam was in January, and equilibrium was the unit he'd been afraid of since September, because it refused to behave like the rest of the subject. Everything before had been arithmetic, cause and effect. This was a system that pushed back.

Kalan leaned over from the next station, chin on his fist. "Ten bucks says the warm one goes pink," he said. "Heat cooks things, right? Hot water breaks stuff down. It'll fall apart to the left." He said it with the ease of a boy who had never once lost a bet on a football field, though chemistry was another country entirely.

Florence didn't look up from her notebook. "Fall apart to the left," she repeated, flat. "That's not a reason, that's a metaphor." She and Kalan had been circling each other since grade ten, each half admiring and half distrusting the other's confidence, and Elijah usually stood between them like a border town.

Elijah looked at the two beakers. On the sill, the blue had begun, faintly, to bleed toward violet, then past violet into a pink he hadn't expected. By the door, the solution held its blue like a held breath. He wrote it down, then crossed out the word "weird," then wrote it again in the margin where crossing out couldn't absolve him of having thought it.

"It's pinker," he said at last. "The warm one. So if pink means products, then heating pushed it right, not left." He said it slowly, because he was assembling it as he spoke, the way he did in the half-dark of his room with a guitar he would never be a virtuoso on, fitting chords together until they stopped arguing.

Kalan shook his head. "That's backwards from everything. Fire destroys things."

"No," Florence said, and now she did look up. "Think of it like this. Some reactions soak up heat when they go forward. If this one does, and you add heat, the system eats it. Uses it. Goes forward." She tapped the beaker on the sill. "If the forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the products. It's in the textbook, page 214, but I didn't believe it until now." She paused. "Kalan, you owe him ten dollars."

"Your metaphor lost," Elijah said, and regretted it immediately, because Kalan's face did something small and closed. They had been friends since Kalan's family moved in two streets over, back when Elijah still thought of this city as foreign and Kalan, born here, autochthonous in a way Elijah's accents and his mother's cooking were not. Kalan had taught him which bus to take, which corner to avoid. Elijah did not want to be right at him like this.

"Here," Elijah said instead, pulling the beaker off the sill and setting it on the counter beside the cold one. "Watch." The pink faded over the long minutes of last period, sinking back through violet toward blue as the solution cooled, and Kalan watched it with his arms folded, then unfolded them, then leaned in. "So it goes back," Kalan said. "Both ways. It's not breaking, it's, like, leaning."

Mr. Crowchild drifted over, hands in his pockets, and looked at the two beakers without touching either. "Which one's the virtuoso now?" he asked, nodding at their notebook full of crossings-out, and walked away before anyone could decide whether it was a joke or a compliment.

Elijah copied the observations twice, once for himself and once for Kalan, whose handwriting fell apart when he was annoyed. He still wasn't certain of everything; he couldn't have said why the system leaned the way it did, only that it did, and that the evidence sat cooling in front of him, refusing to be a metaphor. Kalan paid the ten dollars in quarters and dimes counted out onto the bench like a penance, and at the door he stopped.

"Same bet on the exam question?" Kalan said. "Double or nothing."

Elijah pocketed the coins and said, "Get your own beaker."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: The DASH diet, short for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension, was tested in a US trial funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and published in 1997.
story:
Blake's grandfather had come home from the clinic on Tuesday with a slip of paper and a word he could not pronounce. The paper said 148 over 92. The word, when the grandfather attempted it, came out something like "dash," which made him laugh, because he thought the doctor was telling him to run. Blake had said he would look it up, mostly to end the conversation, and then had not looked it up for two days.

On Thursday Mr. Lombardi kept him after the health elective. The room smelled of the chlorine wipes the janitor used on the desks, and the blood pressure cuff on the counter was still out from the day's practicum. "You missed the cutoff on the practical," Mr. Lombardi said. "You took the reading fine but you couldn't tell me what it meant or why. Monday you retake it. You'll explain the numbers and you'll explain what changes them." He did not sound angry. He sounded like a man handing over a job.

Blake found Harrison in the library that afternoon, spreading peanut butter on a bagel with the plastic knife from his lunch bag. Blake sat down across from him and opened his notebook. "I need the cuff stuff," he said. "The top number and the bottom one." Harrison finished chewing before he answered, which Blake took as a courtesy, since Harrison usually talked through food. "Pressure when the heart squeezes, pressure between beats. Top one first. You wrap the cuff, pump it up past where you stop hearing the pulse, then let it out slow and listen." He tapped his own wrist. "It's not a mystery. It's plumbing."

"Then why does my grandfather's number matter?" Blake said. "148 over 92. The doctor put him on some diet and told him to walk. Is that medicine or is that homework?" Harrison shrugged. "You're asking the wrong guy. I got a 91 in that class by memorizing the order of the steps." He folded the bagel around the peanut butter and stood up. "Simeon's in the weight room if you want someone who reads."

Simeon was doing calf raises in the corner of the weight room, a textbook balanced on the safety bar of the rack. Blake asked him the question straight out: did diet actually move blood pressure, or was that something adults said the way they said breakfast was the most important meal. Simeon set the weight down. "Depends what you mean by actually." He pulled a towel off his shoulder. "There's the stuff your grandmother believes, and there's the stuff somebody tested. My mother maligns salt constantly, and she might be right, but she can't tell you where she learned it. That's the difference. She has the conclusion without the receipt."

Blake wrote "receipt" in his notebook, then crossed it out, not knowing what he meant by it. That night he sat at the kitchen table with his laptop while his grandfather watched a game show in the next room. He typed the word from the slip of paper, the one the doctor had written in the margin: DASH. The first result was a study. The diet the doctor had named was not a brand anyone was selling. It stood for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension, and it had been tested in a US trial funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the results had been published in 1997. Blake read the sentence three times. His grandfather was being prescribed something with a trial behind it, a receipt, and neither of them had known.

"Grandpa," Blake called. "It's called DASH. It's not about running." His grandfather appeared in the doorway with his glass of water. "Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. It's a diet they actually tested." His grandfather looked at the screen over Blake's shoulder. "In 1997," Blake said. "Somebody paid for the study. It wasn't a guy selling a book." His grandfather was quiet for a second. "So it's not just the doctor being careful with me." "It's not just that," Blake said.

He spent an hour building a grocery list with his grandfather, translating the diet into food the man would actually eat. Canned soup went off the list and low-sodium versions went on, under protest. Blake drew a walking route from the apartment to the pharmacy and back, timed it at twenty minutes on the map, and wrote "twice a day" beside it. His grandfather said the route passed the bakery, and Blake said they would discuss the bakery.

On Monday Mr. Lombardi set up the cuff at the practicum station and sat across the desk with his clipboard. "Fifty-eight-year-old male, reading of 148 over 92. Tell me what you're seeing." Blake wrapped the cuff on Harrison, who had volunteered as the patient, and worked the bulb while he talked. "Top number is the pressure when the heart contracts, bottom is between beats. This reading is elevated. The patient's doctor started him on a diet called DASH." He paused to listen for the pulse, watched the needle, read off Harrison's actual numbers, which were enviably boring, and kept going. "Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. It was tested in a US trial funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, published in 1997. Plus walking, twice a day, twenty minutes."

Mr. Lombardi wrote something on the clipboard. "And does it work?" Blake thought about the question. He had the study, and he had his grandfather, and on Saturday the old man had walked the route once, past the bakery and back, and reported a number of 146 over 90, which was one point of change in a direction nobody could prove meant anything yet. "The trial says yes," Blake said. "My grandfather says we'll see. I'm somewhere between." Mr. Lombardi looked up from the clipboard and held his eyes for a moment. "That's the answer," he said. "Retake passed. Send in the next one." Blake unstrapped the cuff from Harrison's arm and wound the tubing around the gauge.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky concluded that basketball shooters' streaks were no more common than chance, calling the 'hot hand' a fallacy.
story:
The chain-link fence behind the west basket still held the dent from last summer's storm, and Luke caught himself staring at it while Preston talked, because it was easier than looking at the scoreboard. They were down four with six minutes left in a park-league game that nobody was keeping stats for, which meant, Preston insisted, that the only stat that mattered was the one everyone could see.

"Eshaan's hit three in a row," Preston said, gesticulating at the far sideline where Eshaan stood wiping sweat off his forehead with the hem of his shirt. "Feed him. Every time down. That's just physics."

"That's not physics," Luke said.

"It's momentum. It's the hand. The hot hand."

Luke had spent a Sunday afternoon two weeks earlier reading about exactly this, not for school, but because he'd gotten stuck on the question of whether a feeling could be true. He'd been looking up something about coin flips, and he'd found a study from 1985, by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone, and Amos Tversky, which concluded that basketball shooters' streaks were no more common than chance. The study called the hot hand a fallacy. He'd read the phrase four times, half hoping he'd misunderstood it, because he had watched Eshaan bury eleven straight free throws in a driveway game in June and he refused to believe that had been nothing.

"Nobody's saying he isn't hot," Luke said now, jogging backward as the ball came inbounds. "I'm saying hot might not mean what we think it means."

"You're saying words."

The game had gone like this all season, and the season itself had gone like this inside Luke: two ways of watching the same player. Eshaan was mercurial, brilliant for stretches and then ordinary, and when he was brilliant the whole team leaned toward him like plants toward a window. Luke felt it too, the certainty that the next shot would go in because the last three had. What he couldn't tell, and it bothered him the way a loose tooth bothers you, your tongue returning to it whether you want it to or not, was whether the feeling was knowledge or just a feeling with confidence attached.

On the next possession Preston threw the pass anyway, a skip pass across the lane that the defender picked off. The other team scored, and it was six, and Preston came back down the court with his hands open, asking the air what it wanted from him.

"He was open," Preston said at the timeout, when Ms. Diallo, who coached the park league every August and ran a hardware store the rest of the year, drew a play in the dirt with her sneaker. "You saw it. He was open because they're scared of him."

"They sagged off because they think he's hot too," Luke said. "Everybody's making the same bet."

Preston squinted at him. "And what do you bet?"

Luke didn't have an answer that fit in a timeout. He had a study, and he had eleven free throws in June, and he had the fact that a shooter's touch is a real thing, that some nights the ball sits differently in your hand, and he could not make those two truths lie flat next to each other. Maybe the streaks were no more common than chance and some nights still felt chosen. Maybe both. The whistle blew before he could say any of it.

What he could do was test it, badly, in the only laboratory available. For three possessions he watched Eshaan without listening to the feeling. First possession, Eshaan took a contested three and missed, and Preston groaned like a man betrayed. Second possession, Luke drove and kicked it to him anyway, not because of the streak, or maybe exactly because of it, he honestly couldn't separate the motives afterward, and Eshaan hit a pull-up from the elbow. Third possession, Luke took the shot himself, off a screen, and banked it in so ugly that the crowd of nine people made a sound like a crowd of ninety.

"Okay," Preston said, chest heaving. "Okay. So he's not hot, and you are?"

"I don't know what I am. I know the study says the streaks aren't more common than chance. That's all it says. It doesn't say what to do with the ball."

Ms. Diallo, within earshot, said nothing, only looked at Luke with something he chose to read as approval, though it could have been amusement. Down three, twenty seconds left, they came out of the huddle with no plan except the one they'd had all game, which was to trust whichever truth they happened to be standing inside.

Eshaan waved for the ball at the top of the key, and the defender gave him four feet of respect, and Luke held the ball a beat longer than he should have, caught between the statistics and the eleven free throws and the fact that Preston had already started cutting. The clock showed nine. Somewhere behind the fence a little kid was shouting, "Shoot it, shoot it, shoot it," and Luke still hadn't decided who was right.

He threw the pass.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Five US states, Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon, have no statewide sales tax.
story:
The paycheque lay on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and a bowl of orange peels, and Grayson had been staring at it long enough that the numbers had started to feel like a language he almost knew. Gross pay, two hundred and eighty-four dollars. Net pay, something closer to two hundred and thirty. In between sat a column of small subtractions, federal income tax, provincial-looking words like CPP and EI, each one taking its quiet share before the money ever reached his bank account. He had earned the gross. He would spend the net. The difference was already gone, spoken for by parties he had never met.

"Twenty-two, twenty-three," Sara-Maude said from the other side of the table, counting coins from her canvas bag. "Also, you look like you've been transfixed by a ghost."

"I've been transfixed by line three," Grayson said. "Who is CPP and why is he in my money?"

She leaned over and squinted at the slip. "My dad calls it the price of having a job. Everybody pays in and someday it pays back. Supposedly."

"That's a very long someday."

"Everything with the government is a long someday," she said, and stacked the quarters. She had come over to plan, not to sympathize. Her own money, saved from two summers of walking dogs, was destined for a laptop, and she had spread printouts across the table like a general's maps. "Here's the thing. The one I want is nine hundred and eighty dollars. With tax it's over eleven hundred."

Grayson pulled one printout toward him. The advertised price had a small asterisk beside it, and below, in fine print, the final price with sales tax added at the register, seven percent, a number that turned almost ninety dollars into the government's share of her laptop. He thought of his paycheque, how the gross number was a fiction you were briefly allowed to believe in.

"So don't buy it here," he said. "My uncle used to talk about this. Delaware has no sales tax. Neither do a few others. Alaska, Montana, New Hampshire, Oregon. Five states, no statewide sales tax at all." He tapped the table. "None. You walk in, the price on the tag is the price you pay."

Sara-Maude went still, which for her was remarkable. "Delaware is four hours from here."

"So? Four hours, ninety dollars saved. That's better than my hourly rate."

"That's not how math works for a sixteen-year-old without a car, Grayson."

"Details," he said, though the details were, he had to admit, fairly germane. No car, no license for highways after dark, and a bus ticket that would eat a third of the savings before she even reached the state line. He turned the paycheque over and did the arithmetic on the back, the honest kind where every cost got a row. Gas or bus fare, lunch, the argument with her mother. The ninety dollars shrank to maybe forty, and then to nothing at all.

Sara-Maude was quiet for a moment, chewing the end of her pen. "My grandmother lives in Oregon," she said slowly. "The one who keeps sending me postcards of mountains. She's been asking me to visit for two years. If I flew out this summer and bought the laptop there..."

Grayson looked up. He had been so fixed on the map, on the line across the state line, that he had forgotten the country had two edges. "Wait. Is Oregon one of the five?"

"Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, Oregon," she recited, reading off the notes he'd scrawled. "You just said it. Five states." She was already reaching for her phone, already composing a message to her grandmother, and Grayson watched the plan reorganize itself around a person instead of a border. The savings would go into a plane ticket, which was not savings at all, but the laptop would be bought in her grandmother's kitchen, presumably, with tea, and postcards of mountains she had actually seen.

He slid the paycheque back toward himself. Two hundred and thirty dollars, net. The deductions had taken their share and would keep taking it, every pay period, forever, and somewhere in that system was a substrate of things he was apparently funding: roads, someone's someday pension, the whole long someday. He couldn't decide whether it felt like theft or like membership, and he suspected the honest answer was that it was both at once, and that he wouldn't know the ratio for years.

"There's still a twist, you know," Sara-Maude said, grinning at her phone. "Grandma just replied. She says she already ordered the laptop. From a store in Delaware."

Grayson laughed so hard he knocked the quarter stacks over. "Then tomorrow," he said, "we calculate shipping," and he turned the paycheque over to its blank side.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
The video arrived in the group chat at 11:47 on a Tuesday, while Christopher was folding laundry in the living room because his mother had finally surrendered the couch cushions to him. It showed a warehouse on fire, men running, a caption claiming the blaze had started that morning at a power station two towns over. Angad had sent it with a single flame emoji. Craig had sent it again twenty minutes later, as though repetition made it truer, and then a third time with the words "should we tell people?"

Christopher watched it four times. The fire looked close, the kind of close that makes you check your own window for orange light. His thumb hovered over the forward arrow, a group of forty-one kids from school on the other side of it, everyone's little siblings downstream of that. Then he put the phone face-down on the folded towels and it buzzed twice more against the terry cloth, insistent as a trapped moth.

He picked it up and, instead of forwarding, opened the browser on his phone and typed "check where a video came from." That was how it went sometimes; you didn't learn a thing until the moment the thing was needed, and then the knowledge appeared as if it had been standing behind you the whole time, waiting to be turned around and faced. He found an article, then a tool, then a page describing a plugin called InVID-WeVerify, built by a European Union-funded project, which splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched. He remembered Angad mentioning it once, back in spring, at his father's office where a colleague had shown them the plugin on a wide monitor, and Christopher had mostly been eating the colleague's biscuits. The memory resurfaced now like something dragged up from the bottom of a lake, dripping, half-recognized. He downloaded it onto his laptop, which sat on the coffee table already open, its fan clicking in the quiet.

The plugin did what the page promised. He pasted the video's link, and it carved the footage into key frames, still images frozen at intervals, and offered them up for searching. He picked the frame with the clearest view of the warehouse, a metal sign legible above the burning doorway, and fed it to a reverse image search. The smell of dryer heat still hung in the room, and somewhere the washing machine thumped into its second spin.

The results loaded in a slow coil. The sign appeared on a news site, dated four years earlier, in a language he didn't recognize. Another hit, a fact-checking page, used the same frame and called the fire an industrial accident from 2021, in a country an ocean away. He checked a second key frame, then a third, and they all snapped back to the same distant year, the same foreign skyline. The video was not this morning. It was not even this continent. His ears felt warm, the specific warmth of having nearly done something stupid at scale.

He typed into the group chat: "Don't forward that." Craig answered immediately, three dots appearing and vanishing, appearing and vanishing, a man thinking hard in public. Then: "why not." Christopher pasted the fact-check link. Then, because a link alone convinces nobody, he typed: "the plugin is called InVID-WeVerify, it splits the video into key frames you can reverse-search." He reread it. It sounded like the biscuit colleague had written it, which was fine, which was maybe the point; the tool didn't care who was borrowing it.

Angad replied first. "so it's old?" Then: "I got it from my cousin." Then nothing for a while, the chat sitting there open like a door nobody had closed. Christopher imagined the video still traveling, pocket to pocket, a virulent little thing that would keep spreading whether or not he had caught it, forty-one kids minus one, minus two. Maybe that arithmetic mattered and maybe it didn't. He could not see the whole shape of it from here, and he was honest enough with himself to admit that: he had checked one fire, on one night, and the town was still full of screens.

His mother came in carrying a mug, looked at the laptop, looked at him. "You've been quiet in here."

"Checking something," he said. He turned the screen toward her, the two images side by side, today's panic and four years ago's accident, identical down to the smoke. She squinted at them for a long moment, sipped, and said, "So it's a lie."

"It's a rerun," he said. "Somebody resuscitated it." She made a small sound, almost a laugh, and went back toward the kitchen, and Christopher sat with the hum of the dryer and the mug's fading steam on the air, Craig's three dots pulsing again at the bottom of the screen.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: In the United Kingdom, government bills are drafted by lawyers in the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel before being introduced to Parliament.
story:
Lucas set his bag down by the chair and slid the stapled pages across the table before he even sat, as though the paper might cool off, like food that had to be eaten while hot. His mother put the serving spoon back in the potatoes and looked at the header: Draft Bill, Lakes and Rivers (Swimming Access) Bill. His father reached for it first.

"That's what we fought about all afternoon," Lucas said. "Model parliament. Ms. Quinn split us into parties and we had to take a bill all the way through, the whole thing, like the real one at Westminster. First reading, second reading, committee, report, third reading, then the votes, then royal assent, the Queen or King signing it and it becoming law. Marvin's party got theirs through. Ours died in committee." He pulled out his chair. "Can I have the potatoes."

"You can have them after you explain why a bill about swimming access has nine clauses about liability," his father said, still reading.

"That's the thing." Lucas sat down and served himself anyway. "We thought arguing would be the hard part. Caelan wrote the actual draft, because he'd volunteered, and he came in with this thing that said everyone should have the right to swim in any lake, period. It took us an hour to figure out that a right with no limits isn't a law, it's a wish. What about private land? What about reservoirs? What about the guy whose cows drink at the river and now sixty teenagers are doing cannonballs off the bank? Every fix made another hole. The wording kept collapsing. It was like entropy, honestly. We'd patch one clause and two others would come apart."

His mother passed him the beans. "So how do real people manage it? Surely Members of Parliament don't sit around with staplers."

"They don't, that's what I found out." Lucas had his phone out under the table before remembering the rule, then put it on the table openly, screen up, his notes visible. "I looked it up when I got home, because Caelan said the government can't just wing a bill either. In the United Kingdom, government bills are drafted by lawyers in the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel before being introduced to Parliament. That's the actual office. Professional drafters, lawyers, whose whole job is the language. Before it even reaches Parliament. So the Prime Minister might stand up with some big idea, but the idea arrives as words written by people whose skill is exactly the thing we were terrible at." He glanced at his father, who had gone a little still. "Anyway. Committee is where ours fell apart. Marvin stood up and read out clause four and asked what the word 'reasonable' was doing there without a definition, and nobody had an answer, because Caelan had put it in at eleven at night to make the sentence feel finished. We voted on amendments and lost, then we lost the clause, then we lost the vote on the whole bill. Twelve to nine."

"That sounds like a decent afternoon's work," his mother said. "You learned where laws actually get made. Not in the shouting. In the sentences."

Lucas pushed a bean around his plate. He had been ready to come home furious at Marvin, and had rehearsed the argument on the walk, the way he could prove the committee had been rigged because Marvin's party had the numbers before debate even started. But somewhere past the corner shop the anger had gone thin, and what he kept thinking about instead was that the shouting was the part he was good at. He liked second reading, the big clash of positions. He'd given a speech about access to open water as an affective thing, a matter of what wild swimming meant to people, not just a policy point, and it had landed; he'd watched it land. And then the bill had gone to committee and died of its own sentences. He could not decide whether the lesson was that the real work was undramatic and he should learn to do it, or whether the drama mattered too, whether a perfectly drafted bill nobody believed in would pass into law and change nothing. Both felt true. He didn't say either one out loud, because at sixteen he had learned that saying a thing like that at dinner usually got it simplified back to him.

"There's a twist," he said instead. "You want the twist?"

His mother said, "There's a twist?"

"So after it died, Ms. Quinn took Marvin's bill, the one that passed, and read us its best clause, the one that won over the swing votes, about managed access points with signage and volunteer stewards. Really elegant. And she said, 'Guess who wrote it.' And Marvin went red. He'd shown it to his uncle before the session. His uncle works as a lawyer in the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel. The actual government drafters. Marvin didn't tell anyone, he just sat there in debate telling us our clauses were sloppy while his came out of that office." Lucas laughed, one short breath through his nose. "Ms. Quinn said it wasn't cheating, technically, because in real life ministers' bills are written by those lawyers before introduction anyway, so Marvin's party was just more realistic than ours. Caelan wants to file a motion of censure at the next session. I told him I'd second it and then vote against it, and he called me a traitor, which, fair."

His father put the draft bill down and turned his water glass a quarter turn, the way he did when deciding something.

"Lucas," he said. "Before you go after Marvin for having help."

"What?"

"I proofread that too." His father tapped the elegant clause Marvin had supposedly stolen from Whitehall. "Marvin's my colleague's nephew. He brought it round Sunday. I moved 'reasonably practicable' from clause six into clause four and cut a comma that was doing the opposite of what he wanted. His uncle never saw it."

Lucas looked at the page, then at his father's hand resting beside it, and heard again the sound of the committee vote, twelve hands rising around a classroom while rain streaked the windows.

"You're going to have to testify," he said.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995; its lead designer was James Gosling.
story:
The computer lab smelled of warm plastic and the janitor's lemon cleaner, and Michael had been staring at the same twenty lines of code for ten minutes. His task was small enough to hold in one hand: build a class in Java with private fields, write getter methods for each one, then test it. Ms. Ba had written the requirements on the whiteboard in her tidy, slanted print, and beneath them a single sentence he kept rereading: the object should protect itself from careless hands. He didn't know yet what that meant. He only knew his file wouldn't compile, and the red underline under `private String name` looked like an accusation.

"You're hovering," said Jericho, sliding into the chair beside him with a granola bar already half unwrapped. Jericho wanted this lab period to be over so he could get to the robotics room before the good batteries were claimed, but he had a habit of sitting down anyway. He leaned over Michael's screen, chewing. "You typed a period where a semicolon goes. Line eleven."

Michael found it. A period, small and round and entirely wrong, sitting at the end of a method declaration like it belonged there. He deleted it and the red underline vanished, and the program compiled with a soft click that felt undeserved. "That's it? That's all it was?"

"That's usually it," Jericho said. "The computer's not mysterious. It's just literal." He checked the clock, then didn't leave. He broke off a piece of the granola bar and set it on the edge of Michael's keyboard, next to the mouse pad, where it wouldn't get crumbs in the keys.

The class Ms. Ba wanted was called `Student`, and Michael made its fields private one by one: name, grade, an ID number. Then, at her instruction, he wrote getters, small public methods that handed back each value without letting anyone change it. He typed a test in the main method, created a student named after himself, printed the name. It worked. He sat back and felt something he couldn't yet name, and it bothered him that the whole thing seemed both obvious and strange. If the fields were his own invention, why hide them behind methods? Why not just let the test reach in directly? He raised his hand, then lowered it, deciding he'd rather figure it out than ask and be handed the answer.

At the next table, Melissa was typing fast, the way she did when she was ahead of everyone and pretending not to be. Her want that afternoon was a specific one: to finish the extra credit version before the period ended, because finishing early was the only reliable pleasure she'd found all semester. But she kept glancing at Michael's screen, and finally she rolled her chair over. "You're doing that thing," she said. "The face. Like the code insulted your family."

"It's the private thing," Michael admitted. "Ms. Ba said the object should protect itself. From what? I'm the one who wrote it."

Melissa considered this, chewing the end of her pen. She didn't give him the answer she'd written in her notes. Instead she said, "Make the ID number public for a second. Change it from the test. See what happens." He did, and the test blithely set his student's ID to negative four hundred, and the program accepted it without complaint, and something in him turned over. The object had stood there and let itself be vandalized. He changed it back to private and added a line in the getter that made him quietly proud: a check, so the ID could never be read out wrong. It was a small wall around a small house, but it was a wall he'd chosen to build.

"You know who made this?" Jericho said, still there, still watching the clock and not moving toward it. "Java. Sun Microsystems put it out in 1995. James Gosling was the lead designer." Michael stared at him. "Older than us," Jericho went on. "At the robotics meet last month a kid from Central couldn't believe it. He thought the language was, like, new. Older than we are and people are still arguing about it." Michael looked at his screen with different eyes after that. The word `private` had been decided before he was born, by a man he'd never meet, and here Michael was at sixteen discovering the reasoning as if for the first time. Maybe that was what an inheritance was: a solution you had to work out again to actually own.

He thought about his father, furloughed from the plant since March, who spent his mornings applying for jobs and his afternoons fixing neighbors' lawnmowers for free. His father had opinions about walls, mostly that too many people built them out of meanness. But this wall, Michael thought, wasn't like that. It didn't exclude anyone; it welcomed them through the door he'd designed, the getter, and only through that door. His father's generosity and Gosling's privacy didn't seem like opposites anymore, though he couldn't have said exactly how they fit together, and he was honest enough with himself to leave that unresolved. Both of them, maybe, were about deciding how you let the world touch you.

Ms. Ba walked the aisles and paused behind him. "Your test coverage," she said, tapping the screen where he'd written a case for a student with no name at all. "Did you mean to include that?"

"Kind of," Michael said. "The object should still work even if somebody makes a mess of it." She looked at him for a moment longer than necessary, then moved on without comment, which from her was a kind of applause. Melissa rolled back to her own station, and Jericho finally stood, brushing crumbs from his jeans, the robotics batteries forgotten or at least forgiven. At the door he turned around.

"Hey," Jericho said. "Tomorrow, teach me the private thing. I still don't get it."

"Bring a granola bar," Michael said, and hit run one more time, watching the name print itself, clean and guarded and his.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Soviet Union refused Marshall Plan aid and pressed Eastern European governments, including Czechoslovakia, to withdraw after first showing interest.
story:
Robert had the two books open on the library table like contestants in a match nobody had agreed to referee. One, by a historian named Halloway, argued that the United States had driven the Cold War into being, that American economic ambition dressed itself in the language of rescue. The other, by a woman named Ostrowski, held that Soviet intransigence came first and the West merely answered it. His essay was due Friday, and his teacher's only instruction, scrawled beneath the prompt, was: test each claim against evidence. That instruction was the problem. Robert had opinions, plenty of them, but he had never once checked whether they could survive contact with a primary source.

He spread his notebook between the books and started a grid. Halloway's column, Ostrowski's column, evidence along the bottom. Beside him, Tess dropped into the chair with a stack of her own books and a can of soda she clearly wasn't supposed to have indoors.

"You look morose," she said. "Histories of the Cold War do that. It's all weather systems and mistrust and nobody ever does anything on purpose."

"That's the question, though. Whether anyone did anything on purpose." He tapped Halloway's page. "He says the Marshall Plan was a weapon. She says it was a shield. I can't tell which because I don't actually know what happened when it was offered."

Tess leaned over. On the map in Halloway's book, Western Europe was shaded in careful blocks and everything east of Austria was blank, white as an unwritten page. "Why is Eastern Europe empty?" she asked. "Did nobody need money there? Half of Poland was rubble."

"I don't know," Robert admitted, and the admission bothered him more than the essay did.

He went to the reference desk, where a man he half recognized was sorting returns. It took him a moment to place the face: Mr. Ma, who lived three doors down from his parents and who had once, years ago, helped drag a branch off their driveway after a storm. He worked here, apparently, on weekdays.

"Where would I find newspapers from 1947?" Robert asked. "Like, actual papers from then."

Mr. Ma didn't deliver a speech about archives or the nature of memory, which Robert had braced for. He simply walked him to a bank of drawers, pulled a reel of microfilm, and showed him once how to thread it and turn the crank. Then he went back to his returns. Robert sat at the viewer and watched the war's aftermath scroll past his face in reversed greys, headlines about coal, about harvests, about a loan from Washington.

He found it in the second session of scrolling, and it stopped him the way a rock stops a plow. The article described the American offer of aid, then reported that the Soviet Union had refused Marshall Plan aid for itself. More than that: it said the Soviet government had pressed the Eastern European governments to withdraw their applications, and it named Czechoslovakia specifically, a country that had first shown interest in the aid and then, under pressure, pulled back. Robert read the paragraph twice, then copied the date into his grid. Tess came to stand behind him, and he read the lines aloud in a low voice, because saying them made them feel like evidence rather than like trivia.

"So wait," Tess said. "The blank space isn't because nobody asked. Czechoslovakia asked."

"And was made to take it back," Robert said. He looked at Halloway's column in his notebook, then at Ostrowski's, and neither fit the way he'd expected. Halloway's claim that the plan was a weapon couldn't explain why a country would show interest unless the offer looked genuine from the inside. But Ostrowski's picture of two rigid blocs couldn't survive the fact that the line between them had wavered, that a government had reached across it before being pulled back. He wrote at the bottom of the page: maybe both are describing a real stratum of the thing and neither is describing the whole. Halloway was looking at American motives, Ostrowski at Soviet actions, and the event itself sat underneath both accounts like a layer of rock that two geologists kept describing from opposite sides of the cut.

He carried the notebook back to the table and found Ostrowski's book where he'd left it, and it was only then that he noticed the margins. Someone had written in them, years ago, in pencil gone soft with age. The handwriting was cramped but certain, and beside a passage about the Marshall Plan the note read: "Weapon or shield? False choice. Look at who changed their minds." A later note, in what seemed the same hand but looser, more doubtful, read: "Not so simple. I was too sure at twenty."

The front flyleaf carried a small signature, half erased: D. Ma, 1979.

Robert sat with that for a moment. He looked over at the desk, at the man sorting returns, at the hands that had once hauled a branch off a driveway and, forty-odd years earlier, had written those margins as a student who thought he'd settled the question. It was strange to think of a neighbor as having once been sixteen and certain, and stranger still to see, in the second note, the certainty curdling into something more careful. Robert wondered whether his own grid, with its tidy columns, was the 1979 version of the same mistake.

He went back anyway. Not to the desk, not yet, because he wasn't sure what he'd say. He went back to the microfilm and turned the crank slowly, watching 1947 continue to arrive one frame at a time, letting the pages come at him in their own order instead of the order the two historians had imposed.

"You're still going to have to pick a side," Tess called from the table.

"Maybe," Robert said, still cranking. "Or maybe I just show my work."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, which did not reveal that its author was a woman.
story:
Ms. Schneider put the passage on the board without introduction, the way she liked to, and Daniel felt the familiar dread of being asked to see something he could not see. It was the part where Jane tells Rochester she is not a bird in a cage, that she is a free human being with an independent will. Four sentences. He had read them twice last night and thought them fine, even stirring, and now he suspected that admiring them was exactly the wrong move.

"Apply a critical lens," Ms. Schneider said. "Feminist or Marxist. Choose one and argue from it." She wrote both words on the board and capped her marker. "Ten minutes. Then you defend your reading to a partner."

Daniel chose feminist, mostly because Gia would choose Marxist and he wanted the argument. He underlined independent will, wrote a question mark, and crossed it out. Across the room Gia was already writing fast, her pen digging a groove into the paper, the way she did when she thought she was winning something that had not started yet.

"Marxist is cleaner," she said when they pushed their desks together. Her elbow landed in the middle of his notebook, deliberate as a flag. "Jane is a governess. Governesses got remuneration, technically, wages, but they weren't servants and they weren't family. The whole job is built to keep her in between. That's class, done."

"That's also women," Daniel said. "She's in between because she's a woman with no money. The lens isn't the cage, it's who built the cage." It came out faster than he'd planned, and he heard his own surprise in it.

"So pick feminist, then. Say something."

He looked at the passage again and found he had nothing sharp, only a feeling that both of them were holding different handles of the same door. Ms. Schneider drifted past and read over his shoulder, which made the back of his neck hot. "Interesting," she said, which was either praise or a trap.

That weekend he escaped to his grandfather's house, partly for the lemon cake and partly because his mother had decided the apartment needed "a serious clean," which meant moving all his things. In the front room the bookshelves smelled of pipe tobacco and dust sweetened by age, and on a low shelf he found a fat old edition of Jane Eyre. He opened it to show Gia later, maybe, and stopped at the title page. Currer Bell. Not Charlotte Brontë. He turned the page twice as though the real name might be hiding behind it.

He called Gia from the kitchen, the phone wedged between his ear and his shoulder while his grandfather cut cake behind him.

"Jane Eyre's by Currer Bell," he said.

"Who is that?"

"That's the thing. Charlotte Brontë first published it in 1847 under that name, and the name doesn't tell you the author's a woman." He heard his grandfather's knife pause on the plate and kept going, quieter. "So when people read about Jane wanting an independent will, they weren't even sure a woman wrote it. Nobody knew."

There was a silence on the line long enough for him to hear her television. "Wait," Gia said. "Okay, that changes the Marxist thing too. If she's hiding, it's money and gender at the same time. Who'd publish her otherwise?"

"Nobody," Daniel said. "Or somebody worse." The answer felt too certain the moment he said it, but she didn't argue, which from Gia was close to applause. His grandfather set a plate of cake down in front of him without a word, and Daniel covered the phone. "Did you know? Currer Bell?"

His grandfather smiled into his coffee. "Everybody knew Currer Bell, once."

On Monday Daniel asked to go first, which he never did, his hands flat on the desk to keep them still. "I kept trying to pick one lens," he said, "like they were teams. But Brontë publishes as Currer Bell in 1847 so nobody can see she's a woman, and Jane in the book is a governess who earns wages but isn't free to be either servant or family. The pseudonym and the passage are the same problem. Gender and class delimit her at the same time, from both sides." He paused, waiting for Ms. Schneider to say it was cheating to use two lenses. She only raised an eyebrow and looked at the class, holding the silence out like a plate.

Gia's hand came up. "He stole half my argument." A few people laughed. "Also it's right," she said, in the intransigent tone of someone conceding nothing. "I'm still doing Marxist on the exam, though. Somebody has to."

"Then somebody has to fight you on it Thursday," Daniel said, and Ms. Schneider wrote both their names on the board under the word debate, and underlined it twice.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
story:
The campus tour began under a banner that said DISCOVER YOUR FUTURE, which Liam felt was a lot of pressure to put on a walk. He had signed up mostly because his mother had filled out the form while he was at swim practice, and the deposit was nonrefundable, so here he was, standing in a quadrangle of wet brick with a laminated visitor badge clipped to his jacket. His application had been submitted nineteen days ago. He knew the number exactly, the way you know a number you are trying not to think about.

Marie-Pier from his calculus class was on the same tour, which neither of them had known in advance. She spotted him by the fountain and drifted over, holding the map the admissions office had given her folded into a shape that no longer resembled a map. "I applied here early decision," she said. "So this is either a victory lap or a hostage situation, depending on December."

"I applied regular," Liam said. "Everywhere. Sort of everywhere." He didn't finish the thought, because the tour guide, a senior in a rugby shirt, had begun walking backward while talking, a skill that struck Liam as more impressive than anything on the brochure.

The guide led them past the library, the dining hall, a building where she claimed a Nobel laureate had once taught, and then stopped in front of the admissions office itself, a converted house with porch swings. "Any questions about applying?" she asked, and to Liam's own surprise his hand went up.

"Is it one application? Or do you have to do a different one for every school?"

Marie-Pier made a small sound beside him, something between a cough and pity. "The Common Application," she said, in the tone of someone identifying a very common bird. "It was founded in 1975 with fifteen member colleges. Now it has more than a thousand. You fill it out once. That's the whole point. That's why it's called common."

"You never told me that."

"You never asked. You just sat at your kitchen table for a month looking like you were being audited." She turned to the guide. "He wrote one essay and sent it to nine schools."

"Eleven," Liam said.

The guide laughed and said the office staff called it the great democratization, though Liam wasn't sure a form that still required an application fee per school had fully earned the word. He filed the objection somewhere for later, in the mental drawer where he kept things he couldn't decide about. The tour moved on toward the residence halls.

While the others examined a sample dorm room, its walls delimiting a life that could be his or couldn't, Liam stood in the hallway looking at a corkboard of student photos. He was trying to work out what he actually believed about the whole enterprise. On one hand, his mother was right that a single application spared him ten more weekends of the same essay, retyped and re-mailed like some kind of penance, a reparation he would have owed each college separately in the old days, back when Marie-Pier's older cousin had apparently done exactly that and spoke of it the way veterans speak of winters. On the other hand, the ease of it unsettled him. Eleven applications in an afternoon meant eleven chances to remain vague about what he wanted. The form was ductile; it bent to fit any ambition, which meant it fit none of them precisely. He had checked a box for undecided, and now the word followed him down the hallway.

"I'm going undeclared," Ali said, appearing at his elbow. Ali had flown in from their school's rival district for the same tour, and Liam had recognized him from the debate circuit, where they had opposed each other twice and neither had won cleanly. "Everyone acts like it's a disease. The guide keeps saying 'students who haven't found their passion yet,' like it's lost keys."

"My dad thinks I should know already. He says he knew at sixteen."

"Your dad also probably knew his major before the internet." Ali looked at the corkboard. "I figure the application is just the first thing you send them. There'll be others. Forms, transcripts, taxes. It's a correspondence, not a verdict."

Liam liked that. He still didn't know if he liked this campus, or any campus, or whether wanting a place and wanting an answer were the same thing. Nineteen days, and then a letter, or more likely an email, a yes or a no that would feel total for about a week. He followed the group back out to the quadrangle, where the banner had begun to sag at one corner.

Marie-Pier caught up with him at the tour's end, holding her folded map like a hand of cards she hadn't played. "So," she said. "Was it a victory lap?"

"I'll tell you in December."

She tore the map in half and dropped both pieces in the recycling bin beside the fountain. "Wait for me," she said, and started toward the parking lot.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In a 2011 Stanford study, basketball players who aimed for 10 hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from 7.9 to 8.8 successful shots out of 10.
story:
The laminated sheet Ms. Tesfaye had given them was blank except for seven boxes, one for each day of the week, and by Wednesday afternoon Camille had filled six of them twice over. She sat on the bleachers at the outdoor court with her knee bouncing, pencil hovering over Sunday. Monday ball handling, Tuesday conditioning, Wednesday shooting, Thursday scrimmage, Friday strength, Saturday more shooting, and Sunday, in three attempts at handwriting she had already crossed out, rest. The word looked lazy sitting there alone in its box.

"You're doing the training program thing," Reagan said, dropping onto the bench beside her with a Gatorade she hadn't paid for judging by the way she waved at the cashier through the fence. She had a way of making statements into questions without the upward lilt. "Danica put her rest day on Wednesday. Right in the middle. She says the weekend is when you get the good runs."

Camille turned the pencil over and erased Sunday's third attempt. "Danica also warmed up for four minutes on Tuesday and pulled something in her hip flexor. I'm not doing that."

"So write warm-ups in every box. Twenty minutes, dynamic stuff, the ladder drills Ms. Tesfaye showed us." Reagan leaned over to look at the sheet, close enough that Camille could smell the orange flavoring. "There. Now you have a real program. Coach will accede to anything that has the word dynamic in it."

Camille wrote it in the margin, smaller than the rest, like a footnote. The program was due Monday, and whoever designed the best one, Ms. Tesfaye had said, would get to run it for the whole team through the regional stretch. Camille wanted that more than she had admitted to anyone, including herself, and wanting it was making the boxes feel heavier than seven empty squares should.

The court behind them filled up around four. Some of the JV boys had arrived, and Reagan stood, restless the way she always was during conversations that lasted past a minute. "Coming?" Camille watched them run their warm-up, the one she had copied into every box, and she noticed something that made her stomach dip. Kyrie, their best shooter, the one whose form Danica filmed in slow motion on her phone, was running it too. He was also, she knew from group chats she only half paid attention to, awake until two most nights, in some game or other, his controller glowing under a blanket.

She didn't shoot well that afternoon. Her release felt late, her legs glacial in the third game even though she had followed her own warm-up to the letter, and after she missed her sixth free throw Reagan called a water break and Camille sat down against the fence with her phone.
