She searched for sleep and free throws on a whim, expecting nothing, some forum full of bro science.

The study came up on the first page. She read the summary twice. In 2011, Stanford had basketball players aim for 10 hours in bed nightly, and their free-throw average went from 7.9 successful shots out of 10 to 8.8. She read it a third time, then held the phone out to Reagan without saying anything, the way you hand over evidence.

"Seven point nine to eight point eight," Reagan said slowly, scrolling. "That's almost a full free throw. Per ten." She looked up at Camille over the top of the phone. "Kyrie's averaging like seventy-five percent right now, and he's up until two."

"Everyone's up until two," Camille said. The fact sat between them on the bench like something physical. She thought about her six boxes, all that beautiful structure, the periodization she'd read about at midnight, of course at midnight, her screen the only light in her room. She had planned every drill down to the minute and had planned nothing for the hours that made the drills work.

"Here's your problem though," Reagan said, and she said it kindly, which from Reagan meant something. "You can write rest days and warm-ups in your boxes. You can't write sleep in somebody's box. That's not a drill. That's like, the metaphysics of the whole thing, the part you don't control."

Camille laughed despite herself, and then she pulled the sheet toward her and turned the pencil to the eraser again. She rubbed out Saturday's second shooting session, the one she had been proudest of, and in its place she wrote sleep, aim 10 hrs, and hated how it looked, soft and unspecific next to ladder drills and conditioning. In the Sunday box, under rest, she added the same line. Two half days of it, given back. She thought of Kyrie under his blanket with the glowing controller and understood that her program could put the number in front of him and could not make him close his eyes.

On Monday Ms. Tesfaye read the sheets at her desk while they warmed up, and Camille watched her own shot chart from the weekend lying crumpled in her bag, six misses circled in red ink she'd added herself. When Ms. Tesfaye tapped one sheet and held it up, Camille couldn't tell from across the gym whose handwriting it was, hers or Danica's or someone else's entirely, and she kept shooting, one after another, waiting to find out.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year.
story:
Isaac stood at the kitchen counter with his cap under his arm, cutting the graduation cake his mother had ordered from the Vietnamese bakery on Fairmount, while in the living room Naomy argued with Ajay about whether the diploma folders were actually empty. They were empty. Isaac had checked his in the car, sliding his thumb along the crease, and found nothing inside but the soft nap of red velvet, which meant the real document would come by mail in July, after someone in an office confirmed that he was, officially, finished.

"Isaac, tell Ajay the folders are props," Naomy called.

"They're props," Isaac said, and went back to the cake, because the knife kept dragging through the strawberry filling and pulling the slices crooked. His mother had invited half the street. Ms. Suryanto from next door was already on her second glass of the sparkling cider, and she'd brought a card with a twenty folded inside it, and she kept telling anyone who paused near her that she'd watched Isaac and his sister grow up through the same kitchen window for eleven years.

Ajay came into the kitchen with his phone out. "Okay, so I texted Devon to see if he's coming, and his sister says they moved to Houston in March." He let that sit for a second. "March. Nobody moved in March and told us."

"He was reticent near the end anyway," Naomy said from the doorway. "He stopped sitting with us at lunch like two months before that. I figured he was mad about something."

Isaac set the knife down. He had figured the same thing, or something close to it, that Devon had decided they were people he could afford to lose, and he had let himself be a little insulted by it, and then stopped thinking about it because it was easier. Now he thought about the four of them in grade nine, the roster photo from orientation: Devon, Marisol, that quiet kid called Anton who'd transferred out sophomore year, a girl named Priya who'd just stopped arriving. He counted on his fingers, using the sticky hand, and got roughly thirty kids out of three hundred forty.

"What," Ajay said.

"Nothing. I was doing math." He wiped his hand on his shorts. "Devon, Marisol, Anton, Priya, that whole table from Mr. Okafor's class. It adds up."

Naomy leaned against the fridge. "Adds up to what?"

Isaac had read the number three weeks ago, scrolling late at night with his chemistry notes open and ignored. He'd gone looking for whether his school was good, whether he was lucky, and he'd found it on a government page: the US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year. He'd stared at the number long enough to memorize it and then closed the tab, because it had felt like something he wasn't supposed to be carrying into a month of parties and dorm shopping. "The average graduation rate for public high schools in the US was eighty-seven percent," he said. "For 2021-22. That's the adjusted cohort rate, meaning they track the whole group that started together, kids who transfer, kids who vanish."

"That's a lot," Ms. Suryanto said from behind him, close enough that he hadn't heard her come in. She took the knife and finished cutting the cake in four clean strokes, the way she did everything, without fuss. "In my last school before I retired, we lost students to the river of life. Some to work, some to worse."

"The river of life," Ajay repeated, grinning a little.

"I'm old. I'm allowed." She handed Isaac the plate with the first slice on it. "Eat before your mother notices the cake is uneven."

He ate standing up, and while he ate he tried to hold two thoughts at once without letting either one malign the other. One was that tonight was his, that the four years had been hard in ordinary ways and he had finished them, that a person could be happy without apologizing. The other was that the living room full of laughing people was a filtered sample, that the empty chairs weren't empty by accident, that Devon's silence at lunch last fall had been a whole situation Isaac had walked past. His father called this kind of thinking a morass, told him he could drown in questions that had no answer, just sink slower and slower. But it didn't feel like sinking. It felt like carrying something that was heavy but belonged to him.

"Hey," Naomy said. She'd been watching his face. "You're doing the thing where you go somewhere else."

"I'm here," he said. He looked at the plate, at the crumbs, at the red velvet folders stacked by the window with their nothing inside. "I keep thinking we should have texted Devon sooner. Like maybe if one of us had, in October. I don't know if it would've mattered."

"It might not have," Ajay said. He wasn't being cruel; he was being Ajay, who trusted data more than regret. "Some kids leave no matter what you do."

"Some kids leave no matter what," Isaac agreed, "and some kids leave because nobody knocked." He set the plate in the sink. Through the window, Ms. Suryanto was already back on the porch, and his mother was lighting the candles on the second cake, the backup one, because she'd worried the first wouldn't be enough.

Naomy pulled out her phone. "Devon's sister still has his number current, probably. Want to text him congrats anyway?"

Isaac looked at the blank message field a long moment before he started typing.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Psychologist Robert Zajonc's 1968 experiments showed the mere-exposure effect: people tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often.
story:
The room smelled like floor wax and dry-erase markers, and Daniel chose the desk by the window because it was the only one with a view of anything, which was the parking lot and, beyond it, the water tower with the town's name painted on it in letters he could read from the highway. TROWBRIDGE. He had read that word forty times in the last three weeks, riding past it in the moving truck, then on the school bus he already resented for its route through the industrial park, and now through this glass. He put his bag on the empty chair beside him so nobody would sit there, and then a girl with chopsticks in her hair lifted the bag off the chair and set it on the floor.

"That's my seat," she said. "I mean, it's not, but it was." She sat down. "You're the new one. Daniel, right? They told me to show you where the gym is, but the gym is wherever anyone says it is, so." She opened a paperback with a cracked spine. "Allyson."

"Daniel," he said, and felt stupid, because she had already said that.

Mr. Takahashi came in carrying a stack of photocopies and a coffee thermos, and he didn't introduce Daniel to the class, which Daniel appreciated more than he could have said. Instead he wrote a question on the board: What makes you like something? Underneath it: Unit 3, Chapter 9. The boy across the aisle, a heavyset kid with a pugnacious jaw who had already knocked Daniel's elbow off the shared armrest twice, raised his hand before Mr. Takahashi even turned around.

"Advertising," the boy said. "Andreas, by the way. You'll want to know that, since I'm your lab partner now." He pointed at the seating chart as if it were settled law. "And the answer's advertising. They play a song a thousand times and you buy the album."

"That's the effect without the cause," Mr. Takahashi said, and handed out the photocopies. "Read the first page. Talk to your partner. I'll be honest, I'm grading the talking, not the answers." He sat at his desk and drank his coffee, and the room went to work around Daniel, and Daniel read.

The first page had a photograph of a man in glasses and a paragraph beside it. Daniel read the name, Robert Zajonc, and the year, 1968, and the phrase experiments showed, and then Allyson leaned over and put her finger on the third line.

"There," she said. "That's the whole unit in one sentence. The mere-exposure effect. People like things more just because they've seen them more often. That's it. Zajonc proved it in '68 with a set of experiments and the whole field argued about it for years and it still holds up."

Andreas leaned across both desks. "So if I stare at your face long enough I'll like your face."

"That's the idea," Allyson said. "Exposure first. Liking second. No reasons required."

Daniel looked out the window at the water tower. He thought about the bus route, how the first morning he had counted the industrial park's dead factories and felt his chest tighten, and how this morning, only the ninth ride, he had caught himself looking for the second factory, the one with the faded smokestack, and feeling something loosened when it came into view, something almost like recognition. He had been telling himself it was a sign he was giving up. He said, carefully, "How long does it take? Before you start liking the thing you hated."

The table went quiet in a way that told him they had both noticed something.

"A month, for me," Allyson said. "I moved here in seventh grade. Screamed at my mother about this town for a month, then one day I was walking down Main Street and it was just my street. I couldn't tell you the day it changed." She closed her book. "It's not that the town got better. I'd seen it that many times, that's all."

"That's terrifying," Daniel said.

"It's efficient," Andreas said. "Think of the applications. You could like anything."

"You could be made to like anything," Daniel said. "That's different." He heard his own voice rise slightly and lowered it. "There were people back home I saw every day for ten years. By your logic I should like them best of anyone alive, and I do, and half of them haven't texted me since the truck pulled out. So exposure isn't the whole thing. It can't be. Or the liking doesn't run both directions, exposure in, exposure out, and if that's true then the whole effect is just inertia with better press."

Mr. Takahashi looked up from his coffee, but said nothing, and went back to his photocopies.

"Or," Allyson said, "the friends back home are also getting exposed to your absence, and absence works the same way, and one day they'll like that more." She said it without cruelty, the way someone states a weather forecast. "I don't know. That part's not in the chapter."

Daniel sat with that. He looked at the water tower again, the white letters, the view he had claimed, and understood that in four weeks he would probably find this window ordinary and then, later, his window, and that he could not tell from inside himself which of those would be a choice and which would only be a count of mornings. He picked up his pen and wrote, on the margin of the photocopy, ninth ride, smokestack, felt okay, and drew a small box around it as if it were data.

"Partner," Andreas said, sliding his chair over. "Question two. Name something you hated that you like now."

Daniel kept his eyes on the margin. "I'll tell you in a month."

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Recipients in an email's Bcc field are hidden from everyone else, which is why messages to a long list of people who don't know each other often use Bcc to protect their addresses.
story:
Keira opened the email at 11:47 on a Tuesday night, with her chem notes still open in the next tab, and read it twice. It was from Ms. Chanthavong, who ran the peer tutoring centre where Keira had volunteered since September. The subject line said Schedules for Fall, Please Read, and the body was three brisk paragraphs about confirmed tutors and a reminder that students were expected to show up even during exam weeks. That part was fine. The problem was at the top, where fifty names sat stacked in the To field like a phone book laid open on a counter. Fifty parents, fifty guardians, fifty addresses, and every single one visible to every single other one. Keira recognized maybe six. She did not know the rest at all.

She sat with her hands off the keyboard for a moment. Forwarding the message to Myah took four seconds, and then she regretted it, because the addresses went along too, forty-nine strangers handed to Myah like a stack of mail left on a bus. She felt a small, specific culpability about that, the kind that arrives late and does not accept apologies. Myah replied with a row of alarmed vowels. "why does she have everyone's emails just OUT like that." Then: "is that even allowed." Keira did not know if it was allowed. She only knew it was wrong, or at least wrong enough that her stomach had tightened before her brain had caught up.

She thought about her mother, whose school district sent out a notice two years ago after a staff member did the same thing with a class list; the notice had used the word incident. Keira had been sixteen and had mostly not metabolized it, filing it under adult paperwork, the way she filed most things that arrived in her mother's voice. Now it landed differently. Somewhere in that stack was a father who did not want his email given to forty-nine other households, maybe for reasons nobody would ever state: a custody arrangement, a job, a plain and sufficient wish for privacy. She could not know. That was the part that itched. She was about to make a claim about people she could not see.

She started typing anyway, then stopped, because her first draft began Keira knew as well as Ms. Chanthavong did, which was false, condescending, and exactly the kind of thing that would make a teacher delete the rest. She deleted it. She opened a new tab and searched, not for an argument, but for the vocabulary, and there it was, plain and unglamorous: recipients in the Bcc field were hidden from everyone else, which was why messages to a long list of people who didn't know each other often used Bcc to protect their addresses. Keira read the sentence aloud to her empty room, quietly, so it would stick. It was not a scandal. It was a setting. The whole thing was a setting.

Cody was still awake; she could see his little green dot. She called him instead of typing, because some conversations went better with voices. "You know how everyone's addresses were just sitting there in the To line?" she said. "There's a fix. It's not even hard. You move the list to Bcc." She heard him shift, the creak of his desk chair. "Does the teacher know about it?" he asked, and Keira said, "I don't know. That's the thing. I don't know if she forgot or if she's never had a reason to know." There was a pause, and then Cody, who was usually the one rushing in, said the sentence she needed: "So write it like you're not sure either. Don't correct her. Just tell her what you saw."

The drafting took forty minutes, which felt absurd for a message that would end up being six sentences long. Keira wrote and cut and wrote again. She led with something true and specific: that she'd noticed the full list in the To field, and that she didn't know whether the recipients knew each other. She said she'd read that Bcc hid the addresses from everyone, and that lists like this often used it for exactly that reason. She asked, rather than announced, whether Ms. Chanthavong might consider it for future sends, and she closed with an offer, since the fall schedule needed assembling anyway, to help clean up the distribution list. She read it once more for tone, hunting for anything that could be heard as a lesson delivered downward, and found only a question and a door left open. She sent it at 12:41 and closed the laptop so she would stop refreshing.

The reply came before first period. Ms. Chanthavong wrote the way she spoke in the tutoring centre, direct and slightly formal, no greeting. "You're right, and I should have caught it. I'll move the list to Bcc going forward. Can you come by at lunch? I want to redo the parent contact sheet properly and I'd rather have two sets of eyes." Below that, a single line: "Also, thank you for how you said it." Keira read that last part three times, not because she doubted it but because it rearranged something, and the rearrangement was tectonic in a quiet way: the discovery that you could disagree with an adult, in writing, and have it count as help.

At lunch, Ms. Chanthavong had the contact sheet open on the centre's old laptop, a spreadsheet with columns that had clearly been through three regimes of organization and survived none of them. She slid the laptop toward Keira and pointed at a column of addresses with duplicates. "Half of these people I've never met," she said. "The parents, the grandparents, some aunts. I've been sending everything to all of them, in one big visible pile." Keira pulled a chair around and started sorting, cutting and pasting, and the work was tedious and strangely steadying. "So for the next one," Ms. Chanthavong said, watching the screen, "I take this whole list and put it where, again?" Keira kept typing. "Bcc," she said. "Every address, one line, and nobody sees anybody else." Ms. Chanthavong dragged the column across, hit send on the test message, and they both leaned in to look at her own inbox, where the To field said, simply, the tutoring centre.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Ontario high school students must complete 40 hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma.
story:
Nolan arrived at the community garden at nine with a printed sheet in his back pocket and the vague sense that he was paying off a debt before he knew what he owed. Ms. Whitehead, who ran the food bank plot between the raspberries and the chain-link, handed him gloves and a bucket and pointed at a bed of weeds that had gone tall and, in the wet morning light, almost elegant. He worked without talking for an hour, pulling pigweed and purslane, learning the small taxonomy of invasives by feel: which roots gave, which snapped and came back.

Farrah was already there when he arrived, though he hadn't noticed her at first. She worked two beds over, fast and careless, tossing weeds into her bucket like she was settling a score. At the water break she introduced herself, watched him try to shake her hand with a glove full of dirt, and laughed in a way that made the morning less grim than he'd been letting it be.

"So are you here for the hours too," she asked. "The forty hours. For the diploma."

"I need them," Nolan said. "I'm in grade eleven. I've got time." He said it too quickly, and she looked at him the way people look when they've caught something.

"It's the Ontario Secondary School Diploma," she said. "You can't graduate without the community involvement hours. Forty of them." She said it flatly, like reading a sign on a door. "Aaden's here because of that. He's in grade twelve and he's cutting it close."

Aaden was older, broad-shouldered, lugubrious in a way that seemed less like sadness than like a coat he wore. He was stacking crates of tomatoes at the harvest table, and when Nolan wandered over, Aaden told him the deadline was coming and he still had a chunk of his hours left. "I kept meaning to," he said. "Then it was March, and then it was basically now." Nolan wanted to say something encouraging and found he had nothing, so he carried crates instead.

The afternoon sorted itself into tasks. Ms. Whitehead set them to harvesting for the Saturday distribution, and there was a rhythm to it, snap and place, snap and place, that let Nolan think while his hands worked. He had come here, he admitted to himself, thinking of the hours as a tax, something to expiate before the ledger closed and the diploma was issued. Farrah, though, kept talking to the people who came to the side gate, women with rolling carts, an old man who wanted to know if the tomatoes were the small sweet ones. She gave away the bruised ones first, said they wouldn't keep, and the old man thanked her twice.

"Why do you actually do this," Nolan asked her, later, when they were washing the bins. "You could get your forty hours anywhere."

"My aunt used this place," Farrah said. "Two years. She didn't need anybody's hours." She scrubbed a spot that was already clean. "I know it's not like that for you. It's fine. It doesn't have to be the same."

He turned that over while he rinsed. His father had a phrase about this, something about pure motives versus useful ones, delivered usually over dishes, and Nolan had always filed it under things adults say. But watching Aaden count his remaining hours out loud, pacing the path like a man doing arithmetic that wouldn't balance, Nolan saw the other side of it too. Aaden was here for the least noble reason available and was nonetheless stacking tomatoes that would feed forty households on Saturday. The motive was selfish and the crates were real. Both facts held at once, and he couldn't make them cancel out, and he suspected the inability to make them cancel was the actual lesson, though nobody had assigned it.

Before they left, Ms. Whitehead signed his sheet and asked if he'd be back next week. He heard himself say probably, and was surprised to find he meant it, or at least wanted to mean it, which felt close enough to act on. Aaden was still there when Nolan walked out, standing over the last crate, and Nolan turned back and called to him.

"You know they weigh what you harvest," Nolan said. "You could tell people you moved two hundred pounds of food."

Aaden considered this, then almost smiled. "That's not how the sheet counts it."

"No," Nolan said, "but it's how I'm going to count it."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Social loafing, the drop in effort people make in groups, shrinks when each member's individual contribution can be identified.
story:
Colton had been the last one benched for the away game at Ridgefield, and he had watched the whole second half from a folding chair with a water bottle sweating in his hand. He said nothing on the bus home. But he noticed something: the substitutes who ran the warmups, all shouting and sprinting, went quiet in drills, jogged the recovery laps, disappeared into the pack of jerseys. So did he, if he was honest. Twenty players doing the same drill made it easy to be invisible, and being invisible had started to feel restful, the way a warm bath is restful, until you remembered you were supposed to be getting somewhere.

On Monday the captain, a senior everyone called Big D, showed up with a clipboard and a phone timer and announced that every player would be timed individually on the sprint sets, name and time written down and posted on the fence. Kaila groaned loudly enough for both sidelines to hear. Keira, who kept the stats, stood by the fence with the sheet and called out times in a flat voice, "Bennett, 12.4. Colton, 12.9," and something odd happened without anyone discussing it. The whole practice got faster. Even the warmups got faster. Players who had been coasting behind the group all season were suddenly running like the scoreboard was on.

Colton ran his set, bent over with his hands on his knees, and looked at Keira's sheet. His time from last week, when they had sprinted as one herd with no clock at all, had been 13.8. Now it was 12.9, and he had not felt like trying any harder. He hadn't even decided to. He rolled this around for two days, the way you roll a stone in your shoe, saying nothing because the assistant coach, an irascible man who despised being asked questions before drills, would only snap at him to run.

He found the answer in the library, of all places, while avoiding a history essay. He had gone looking for something about training, about legs and lungs, and instead he found a paragraph in an old social psychology textbook left on the cart, and the phrase jumped out at him like a name he'd forgotten he knew. Social loafing. The drop in effort people make in groups. He read the next line twice: it shrinks when each member's individual contribution can be identified. He sat very still in the library chair. It was not a secret about running. It was a secret about being one of many.

The next practice he tested it, quietly, without pontificating about textbook paragraphs to teammates who would laugh at him. He stood where Keira recorded the times and watched people run. When the clipboard came out, everyone ran hard. When Big D put it away for a scrimmage, half the team went soft again, drifting, letting someone else chase the ball. Colton did the same thing, he realized, drifting on the far wing, letting Kaila take the fifty-fifty balls because Kaila was closer and someone would get it anyway. That was the whole mechanism, or the whole shape of it anyway, and he did not need to know more than the shape.

But a considered position was harder than a discovered fact. Because there was another way he had been thinking, which his father had taught him without meaning to: that the team was a kind of family, that you played for the name on the front, that counting individual times was small and selfish, the sort of thing that belonged in a corporate office and not on a field. And Colton could see how both things were true at once. The clipboard made everyone run faster, and the clipboard also made Big D talk to the slower players like underperformers, made Kaila practice with her jaw set, made everything a measurement. He did not know how to hold both of these at the same time, and he suspected nobody did, that maybe being seventeen was mostly this, carrying two true things that rubbed against each other.

He decided not to decide. Instead he did a smaller thing. On Thursday he asked Keira if he could keep a private sheet of his own times in his sock, before the clipboard came out, when nobody official was watching. She raised an eyebrow at him, sensing there was a reason, and he told her the truth, or most of it, "If I'm only fast when someone's writing it down, I want to know that about myself." She wrote his name at the top of a fresh column and said nothing back, which was its own kind of approval.

The first timed sprint of the season, the one that counted, came in the last minute of the Ridgefield rematch, when the score was tied and the ball spilled loose into open grass and Colton was the nearest player in a red jersey. Nobody was timing it. Nobody would ever know the number. He took off anyway, socks of paper crumpling somewhere, and heard Keira's voice from the sideline, steady and flat, calling out, "Go, Colton."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
The text from Hafsa arrived during seventh period: come over, we need to talk about the relay. Taylor walked the six blocks to Hafsa's house with her bag heavy on one shoulder, rehearsing nothing, which was itself a kind of avoidance. Inside, the kitchen smelled like cardamom from something on the stove, and Lauren was already at the table, arms crossed, pushing a mug in slow circles on the wood.

"Coach told me you want me off the relay," Lauren said, before Taylor had her shoes off.

"I never said that." Taylor pulled out a chair but didn't sit. "I said we have a problem."

Lauren had missed practice twice that week and showed up late to a third, and at Saturday's meet the handoff between them had gone badly, the baton wobbling in the exchange zone while Taylor's arm swung through empty air. Afterward, in the parking lot, Taylor had said something she was already sorry for, something like you never take anything seriously, and Lauren had walked to her mother's car without answering.

Hafsa set down three glasses of lemonade and lowered herself into the chair between them, which was either diplomacy or cowardice, Taylor couldn't decide. "Okay," Hafsa said. "So say the thing you actually came to say."

Taylor sat. She had spent Sunday reading instead of texting an apology, because an apology alone felt like a lie, and she had landed on a page in her mother's book about relationships, a psychologist named Gottman. "I looked something up," she said, feeling peevish about how schoolteacher she sounded. "Gottman calls a complaint something that addresses a specific behavior, and criticism something that attacks the person's character."

Lauren's mug stopped circling. "Which one did I get in the parking lot?"

"Criticism," Taylor said. "I attacked you. I said you never take anything seriously, and that's about who you are, not what you did." She made herself keep going, though the kitchen was very quiet and the cardamom was making her feel like she'd wandered into someone else's family ritual. "The complaint would have been that you missed practice twice this week, and we botched the handoff, and I need you there Thursday."

Lauren looked at the window for a while. Hafsa, mercifully, said nothing at all, just turned her glass so the ice knocked against the sides.

"You know why I missed," Lauren said finally. "My dad's appointments. Tuesday was the biopsy results."

Taylor hadn't known. She had spent the week constructing a story in which Lauren was careless, and it had been easier to malign her than to ask, because asking carried the risk of hearing something she couldn't fix. "I didn't know," she said. "I should have asked before I decided what it meant."

"And I should have texted the coach," Lauren said. "I know Thursday matters. I'm not asking to skip it."

They sat there with the lemonade going warm. Taylor thought about how a rule like complaint-versus-criticism could become its own kind of deterrence, a way of keeping everyone so careful that nothing true got said, and how that would be its own failure, politeness standing in for honesty. But Lauren was looking at her now instead of at the window, so maybe the rule made truth survivable rather than smaller. She held both ideas and couldn't get them to settle into one.

"Can we practice the exchange before Thursday?" Taylor asked. "Even twenty minutes after the team leaves. I'll stay."

"I can do twenty minutes," Lauren said. She picked up her mug and drank from it, finally, like the whole conversation had been something to get through first. Hafsa reached over and clinked her glass against it, and outside a lawnmower started up two houses down, loud and ordinary, filling the kitchen while nobody spoke.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Gottfried Leibniz introduced the integral sign in 1675, basing it on an elongated letter s because he thought of an integral as an infinite sum.
story:
Victoria had told her mother she was going to the tutoring centre because she wanted to raise her calculus mark, which was true in the sense that most things are true if you ignore their context. What she actually wanted was to understand the exam she had failed, which was not the same thing. Raising the mark was a goal; understanding was closer to a grievance. She had gotten the right answers all semester by following procedures and had never once known why they worked, and the exam, sensing this, had punished her.

Mr. Bautista ran the centre out of a strip mall unit between a nail salon and a shop that seemed to monetize loneliness by selling single servings of cake. He had a whiteboard, a kettle, and a policy of never giving anyone the answer. Victoria found this policy specious on day one, when it took her forty minutes to arrive at something he had known all along, but by the second week she had begun to suspect the policy was aimed at her specifically, like a diet.

"Draw the curve," he said now. "Then draw rectangles under it."

"Rectangles are wrong," Victoria said. "The area under a curve is curved. The whole point of a curve is that it isn't a rectangle."

"Draw thin ones."

"Thin rectangles are still wrong. They're just wrong less."

"Wrong less," Mr. Bautista repeated, and she could see he was filing the phrase away to torment future students with, and she hated that she'd given it to him.

She drew thin rectangles, thinner ones, then a sequence so fine the space between them closed like a zipper. Somewhere in there the area stopped being an approximation and became a number, and Victoria experienced this as a small betrayal, because she had spent three weeks defending the position that the whole thing was fake, and now the number sat on her page looking exact.

The kid at the next table interrupted. He was maybe twelve, doing fractions, and he had been eavesdropping with the shamelessness of someone who had not yet learned that listening in costs something. "Why is that sign all stretched out?" he asked, pointing at the long s lying on its side in her integral. "Is it a messed-up two?"

"It's an s," Victoria said, and then, because she honestly didn't know why, she looked at Mr. Bautista, who looked at the ceiling, which was his way of saying she had the tools. She stared at the symbol. It was an s, elongated, sum, the sum of all those rectangles, an infinite sum of areas so thin they were almost nothing.

"It's for sum," she said slowly. "Leibniz drew it like that. An elongated s." She turned to the kid. "He thought of an integral as an infinite sum, so he used the first letter of sum and stretched it out."

"When?"

"1675," said Mr. Bautista, from the ceiling.

"He invented it in 1675," Victoria translated, and felt something settle, not an understanding exactly but a handshake between two things she had been keeping separate: the symbol she copied and the rectangles she drew, which turned out to be the same object viewed from two directions. The notation wasn't decoration. It was a picture of the idea. She had spent a semester treating the mathematics as a symbiosis between memorized shapes and permitted moves, each using the other without either understanding anything, and now the partnership looked different, though she could not yet say how.

The kid nodded and went back to his fractions, where everything was honestly sized and no symbol lay down on the job. Victoria looked at her page again. The rectangles and the stretched s agreed. They would agree tomorrow, when she tried a harder function, or they would not, and she would be back here on Thursday drawing wrongness so thin it became right. That was the part she couldn't verify yet, whether it always worked or only worked the way a borrowed umbrella works, fine until weather.

"One more," said Mr. Bautista, and handed her a fresh sheet.

Victoria uncapped her pen, and at the top of the page, before the numbers, she drew the long slow s.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: The principle called Chekhov's gun, from the playwright Anton Chekhov, holds that anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play.
story:
Felix set his laptop on the kitchen table after dinner and opened a document he had titled, without enthusiasm, Play. The assignment from Mr. Pritchard was a ten-minute play about a moment from his own life, and it was due in nine days. He had chosen the night in eighth grade when he'd found his father sitting in the dark garage at midnight, and had spent three evenings turning it over without writing more than a page.

He typed the first scene. A boy comes home late. He passes the garage. Inside, on the workbench, his father's measuring tape, a coffee mug, a set of keys, a flashlight. The father sits on an overturned bucket with his back to the door. Felix remembered it exactly, because that was the trouble: he remembered everything in that garage and did not know which thing to keep.

In the real garage, the flashlight had been on, aimed at nothing. The measuring tape had been unspooled across the floor, a yellow line in the dust, and neither of them had picked it up. His father had eventually said, "You should be asleep," and Felix had said, "So should you," and they had gone inside and eaten toast at one in the morning and never talked about it again. That was the whole moment. It fit inside ten minutes easily and then left him with nothing to say.

Tyson and Maelly came over on Saturday for a table read, as Mr. Pritchard required, one draft read aloud before rehearsal. They sat in the living room with the pages between them and the plates from lunch still on the coffee table. Maelly read the stage directions. Tyson read the father, dropping his voice in a way that made Felix wince and then, reluctantly, lean forward.

Afterward Tyson tapped the first page. "The flashlight. It's on, aimed at nothing, in the first minute. And the measuring tape unrolled on the floor. Then they never come back. The whole rest is just toast."

"So that's how it was," Felix said. "I'm not making it up."

"Mr. Pritchard's going to eat you alive." Tyson flipped the pages back and forth. "It's called Chekhov's gun. From the playwright Anton Chekhov. Anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play."

Maelly said, "So either the flashlight matters or it shouldn't be there."

Felix looked at the pages for a long moment. "The flashlight was my dad's," he said finally. "He kept it in the kitchen drawer for years after, and when he finally moved out, he left it. I found it when we were packing the kitchen." He had not put any of that in the play. He had not thought about why he'd left the flashlight in the scene except that it had been there.

He tried three drafts that week. In one, the boy in the play found the flashlight again in the last scene, years later, in a drawer, and held it without turning it on. In another, the father picked up the measuring tape and reeled it in, slowly, in the final silence, and that was the ending. Both drafts felt true and both felt arranged, like he had taken a messy night and combed it into a shape the night never had. He sat at the kitchen table on Thursday with the two versions open side by side and could not choose between them.

Maelly read both over FaceTime that night. "The second one's cleaner," she said. "The tape coming back in. It's incisive, like the whole play is one motion." She paused. "But it didn't happen."

"The flashlight one happened. Just not in ten minutes. It happened over three years."

"So cut the toast scene and put the drawer in."

"Then I'm writing a different play." Felix heard his own voice go flat and steadied it. "The night I'm writing about, nothing mattered later in the way a play wants things to matter. He sat there, I stood there, we ate toast. That was it."

Mr. Pritchard had said something the first week that Felix now turned over like a coin with no second face: the assignment wasn't to record a memory, it was to make something that worked on a stage. He had also said the play had to be about a real moment, which Felix had taken to mean true, and he was no longer sure true meant the same thing as accurate. His parents' divorce had been a long mutualism of silence, each of them recuperating in separate rooms, and if he put the flashlight in the drawer at the end, he would be lying about the order of things, and if he took it out of the garage he would be lying about the night itself.

On Sunday he cut the measuring tape and kept the flashlight, but not the drawer. The play ended with the boy turning the flashlight off and standing in the dark for a ten-count before the blackout. At the staged reading on Tuesday, in the school's black box with folding chairs, nobody in the audience of classmates moved during those ten seconds. Afterward Tyson found him by the door. "Still not a gun," Tyson said. "But it worked anyway."

"I don't know if I got it right," Felix said.

Tyson shrugged. "Chekhov's dead. He can't complain." He handed Felix the pages, warm from the lights, and Felix folded them in half and put them in his jacket pocket, where the crease stayed for days.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor; it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
story:
Luca signed up for the foods elective because the room had eight stoves and his mother's shifts at the hospital ended at eight, which meant that on Tuesdays and Thursdays dinner was his problem. Mr. Suzuki's assignment for the final unit was direct: cook a full meal for your family, document it, bring in the leftovers. Luca had tried this once already at home, steaming chicken breast because it seemed clean and safe, and the family had eaten it in silence, his grandfather pushing the pale pieces around the plate like a man remonstrating with a bad chess opponent.

The classroom smelled of vinegar and dish soap. Luca set his pan on the burner and laid out the chicken, salted the night before in the school refrigerator, labeled with his name on masking tape. Katelyn worked two stations down, constructing something with three kinds of mushroom, and Vicky had claimed the station beside his because, she said, she wanted to watch him fail at a protein again.

"Why hot," Luca said, mostly to himself. His grandfather had said only that the pan needed to be hotter, which was the kind of advice that told you the score without telling you the game.

Katelyn, without looking up from her mushrooms, slid a laminated card across the counter. "From the browning unit. Page two."

He read it half aloud. "Between amino acids and sugars, browning food and creating much of its flavor. It proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius." The card had a name for it, which he said out loud because Vicky was watching him. "The Maillard reaction."

"Say it again with feeling," Vicky said.

He was, he supposed, a pragmatist about cooking; he wanted a method that worked every time, not a philosophy. But the card gave him a range, not a method, and he turned the dial to medium because medium felt responsible. He laid the chicken in. It sat in the pan, sweating, turning the color of a thumb after a long bath. Vicky leaned over. "It's steaming again. You're steaming it in a pan now. Innovation."

"It's only been a minute."

"It's been four."

He checked the card, checked the dial, and thought about his grandfather's plate, the pieces pushed around and around. Then he lifted the chicken out, wiped the pan with a paper towel, turned the dial until the element glowed dull orange, and waited, counting under his breath, until a drop of water skated across the surface and vanished. He put the chicken back in, skin side down, and it made a sound like tape being torn, and within a minute it had gone the deep brown of toasted bread, the color he had never once achieved at home.

Mr. Suzuki drifted past, looked at the pan, and knocked twice on the counter with his knuckle, which was, as far as anyone could tell, the highest praise he issued.

Vicky tasted a scrap of the skin Luca cut from the edge. She was quiet for longer than was natural for her. "It actually tastes like something," she said, in the tone of a scientist confirming an inconvenient result.

The full meal, photographed on his kitchen table at home, consisted of that chicken, rice, and green beans he'd seared in the same pan, because the brown bits on the bottom had seemed suddenly valuable rather than ruined. His mother came in still wearing her hospital badge, his sister arrived late from soccer, and his grandfather sat down without comment. Luca watched them eat without saying anything about temperatures or amino acids, because saying it would have sounded like an excuse dressed as a lesson.

His grandfather finished first. He set down his fork, looked at the platter where the remaining pieces sat glossy and brown, and said, "Your grandmother is going to be furious I enjoyed this."

Luca asked why.

"She's been telling me for forty years the pale way is healthier." His grandfather reached over and took a second piece.
